title: A passage through the manuscripts
scope: Three closely followed Greek New Testament passages, a papyrus restoration and a fourth manuscript investigation (GA 304). Early translated traditions are introduced as evidence, not independently collated. Not a statistical sample of the Bible or a survey of Hebrew/Septuagint textual criticism.
authorization: The user's explicit request for completed research, design and implementation supersedes the programme's earlier content-only pass for study 02. No public deployment authorized.
teachingSequence: Separate object, transcription, restoration and critical edition before comparing readings.
Galatians: compare spelling and word order, then decode the real comparative apparatus token by token.
Romans: distinguish hands, then test external attestation, copying mechanism and intrinsic context without assigning artificial probabilities.
Mark: inspect coverage; read each continuation and ask how its narrative joins; distinguish circulation, authorial origin and theological reception.
At the broken edge: restoration does not recover ink.
GA 304: inspect commentary context before treating the last biblical extract as a Gospel ending; follow a research correction.
Optional copying model and P45 assessment test dependence and absence.
Trace changing editorial practice from historical editions through ECM and CBGM; follow primary sources and explicitly labeled reading leads.

displayPolicy.greek: Short selected readings, with accents, case and spaces normalized for comparison unless explicitly labeled diplomatic excerpt. Sacred-name contractions expanded. No attempt at a facsimile or complete diplomatic transcription.
displayPolicy.english: Original explanatory glosses of the selected words; not quotations from a modern Bible translation.
displayPolicy.absence: A non-extant portion has no recoverable reading here. It is never represented as an omission or counted against a variant.
displayPolicy.corrections: First-hand and corrected states belong to the same physical witness. Corrector labels follow the cited apparatus and are not independently redated.
displayPolicy.editions: SBLGNT primary text and comparative apparatus checked. NA28 and historical edition readings are reported through that apparatus, not claimed as an independent full collation of those editions.
displayPolicy.rights: No manuscript photographs reproduced. All diagrams original and explicitly schematic. Short SBLGNT excerpts attributed to Michael W. Holmes, SBL and Logos, 2010, CC BY 4.0; formatting and highlighting adapted. Michigan transcriptions quoted only in short extracts with adjacent attribution.

cases.question: When does a different spelling become a different reading?

witness.shelfmark: Michigan inv. 6238 / Chester Beatty BP II
witness.locator: Codex page 168; Galatians opening lines 5–6 in Michigan's reader
witness.date: Third century, as dated in Michigan's introductory exhibit

evidence.claim: Michigan transcribes υμειν and explains it as reverse iotacism; its normal equivalent is ὑμῖν. Both mean 'to you'.
P46 has καὶ κυρίου ἡμῶν after πατρὸς. SBLGNT prints this order; its apparatus reports ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου for NA28 and Westcott–Hort.

cases.interpretation: The vowel spelling does not change the addressee. Moving 'our' makes it most naturally qualify 'Lord' instead of 'Father'. This is a modest difference in phrasing, not a new identity for either referent.
cases.editorialReasoning: A normalized critical edition can retain a witness's word order while regularizing its spelling. The comparative apparatus documents editorial disagreement; it does not give Holmes's complete local rationale or a manuscript census.
limits: Do not call Michigan's teaching 'standard text' the wording of every critical edition.
Do not infer that agreement at this phrase makes SBLGNT a transcription of P46.
Do not infer a direct copying relationship from one shared reading.

cases.question: A statement or an exhortation?

evidence.claim: NET's textual note reports ἔχωμεν for Sinaiticus first hand and Vaticanus first hand, and ἔχομεν for their cited corrected states (א1, B2).
Sinaiticus project locates Romans 4:12–5:16 on BL folio 262b, scribe A.
SBLGNT prints ἔχομεν; its apparatus reports agreement with NA28 and Robinson–Pierpont, against ἔχωμεν in Westcott–Hort and Tregelles.

cases.interpretation: ἔχομεν is indicative ('we have'); ἔχωμεν is subjunctive (here 'let us have'). A single vowel can alter the force of a clause even though other vowel differences are mere spelling.
cases.editorialReasoning: NET prefers the indicative from the flow of Paul's argument while acknowledging strong external evidence for the subjunctive. Similar vowel sounds offer a possible route of confusion but cannot establish its direction. NET questions UBS4's A-level confidence; this is an attributed disagreement, not a claim about every later edition.
limits: The digital viewer shell was read for the folio locator; its dynamic Greek correction display was not independently collated. Readings are explicitly attributed to NET's apparatus.
No claim that the two correctors worked at the same date.
The small displayed witness selection cannot settle the case by vote.
Correction can preserve a good alternative or introduce a change; 'corrected' does not mean 'original recovered'.

cases.question: Is an absent ending the same as a lost page?

evidence.claim: Sinaiticus ends Mark at 16:8; the project records Mark 16:1–8 and Luke 1:1–18 on BL folio 228, scribe D.
Vaticanus ends at 16:8 with a blank column; Alexandrinus contains 16:9–20.
P45's extant Mark portions belong to chapters 4–9 and 11–12. Mark 16 is not extant; this is no evidence of omission.
SBLGNT's digital text includes both the unnumbered Shorter Ending and 16:9–20 in double brackets.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.10.5, quotes wording from Mark 16:19 as Mark's conclusion; this attests use of the longer ending in the late second century, not a surviving second-century Gospel codex.
The prevailing critical-edition judgment is an earliest attainable ending at 16:8, while the authorial intent question remains distinct.

interpretations.position: Argues for the ending at 16:8, combining early manuscript evidence and the literary difficulties at the join.

Defends the longer ending; emphasizes early reception and broad transmission, proposing that Mark's colleagues attached material by Mark. This is a minority reconstruction; the main critical-edition conclusion is not evenly split between these two essays.

limits: Snapp's proposed composition history is a reconstruction, not a fact written on a manuscript.
A blank column does not by itself establish what a scribe knew or intended.
A surviving ending at 16:8 does not prove that no earlier ending was lost before this copy was made.
This selection is not a full apparatus: the Shorter Ending, translated witnesses and the Freer Logion require deeper study.
Canonical reception and authorial origin are related but different questions; the page does not equate them.
Alexandrinus wording is reported from scholarly accounts; the old BL viewer redirected to an unavailable-images landing page.

cases.question: Are the restored letters actually there?

evidence.claim: Michigan's diplomatic transcription ends the relevant line with θελ[ημα; the bracket marks supplied letters at the broken edge.

display.convention: The desk closes the square bracket for an isolated excerpt, displaying θελ[ημα]; this is an adaptation of Michigan's line-ending notation.

cases.reconstruction: The rest of the word is supplied from linguistic and textual context, not read as surviving ink. Confidence in a restoration does not change its evidential category.
limits: The displayed edge is typographic, not a tracing of the papyrus.
Lacuna means a physical or textual gap; an entire missing leaf has two lost sides. Neither is automatically a copying omission.

method.externalEvidence: Compare dates, distribution, corrections, relationships and actual coverage; copy date is not automatically the age of a reading.
method.internalEvidence: Ask what fits the author's language and what copying process might account for the alternatives. A plausible process is an argument, not an observed event.
method.counting: Surviving descendants of a common source are not independent origins. Neither always choose the oldest nor always choose the majority is a sufficient method. The educational 8-versus-2 copying model is invented, not a genealogy of these witnesses.
method.cbgm: INTF's Coherence-Based Genealogical Method relates variant genealogies and textual witnesses; its results require editorial analysis and do not simply recover a physical family tree of extant books.

researchQuestions: What does each object actually preserve at the location under discussion?
Which differences alter meaning, and which reflect spelling or editorial normalization?
What kind of support does an edition’s apparatus record—and exclude?
Can a copying explanation discriminate between alternatives, or does it work in both directions?
When does a textual ending establish an authorial ending, and when does it expose incomplete production?
How can a scholarly consensus retain its conclusion while revising a supporting witness?

claims.claim: The published Gal 1:3 entry is καὶ κυρίου ἡμῶν Treg RP ] ἡμῶν καὶ κυρίου WH NA28. The bracket separates the printed reading from alternatives; cited sigla here identify editions.
claims.limits: Not a complete manuscript apparatus. The older introduction defines NA26–27; the currently consulted digital entry explicitly says NA28.

claims.claim: The same sound confusion can generate either vowel; it cannot independently determine direction.
claims.limits: A plausible mechanism, not an observed copying event. No inferred dictation event is asserted.

claims.claim: Romans 5:10 presents reconciliation as accomplished; NET uses the argument’s indicative force in preferring ἔχομεν.
claims.limits: Do not equate a preferred contextual reading with an extant autograph.

claims.claim: Mark 16:7 promises a meeting in Galilee; 16:8 describes flight and silence; 16:9 reintroduces Mary Magdalene with the seven-demon detail.
claims.limits: Narrative summaries in original English. The literary significance of the seam is an inference, not a manuscript inscription.

claims.claim: The unnumbered Shorter Ending resolves silence with a report to Peter’s circle and a worldwide proclamation. SBLGNT distinguishes it from stopping at 16:8 and from 16:9–20.
claims.limits: Selected forms only; no complete survey of combined endings or Freer Logion.

claims.claim: To Marinus 1 presents two responses: dispute the ending on manuscript grounds, or accept it and reconcile the resurrection chronology by punctuation.
claims.limits: The work survives through later transmission including an abridgment. Reported prevalence is not a recoverable manuscript census; the author’s precise preference requires interpretation.

claims.claim: Houghton reports the editorial consensus that the earliest attainable text ends at 16:8, reaffirmed by ECM Mark 2021.
claims.limits: Not the same claim as certainty about Mark’s intended conclusion. The site does not adopt Head’s theological inference from non-originality to non-inspiration.

claims.claim: GA 304 is BnF grec 194, a first-half-twelfth-century catena. Its biblical extract at 16:8 is followed by a scholium. Houghton questions its use as a short-ending witness using scribal ending practice, another hand’s erased epigram and commentary dependence.
claims.limits: Analysis followed from published research, not a fresh object inspection. Reason copying ceased is unresolved.

claims.claim: Nestle’s 1898 edition compared editions; Kurt Aland introduced direct manuscript evidence into that edition’s work; Barbara Aland’s directorship supported the ECM collaboration; James appeared in 1997.
claims.limits: This is a selected development, not a history of all textual scholarship or a claim that nineteenth-century editors did not consult manuscripts.

claims.claim: ECM’s published split-guiding-line list includes presence/absence of καὶ νηστείᾳ at Mark 9:29/29.
claims.limits: A concrete example of an unresolved editorial choice; no full manuscript collation or commentary of this passage undertaken.

claims.claim: Mink distinguishes textual states from physical manuscripts and incorporates contamination and possible repeated independent emergence of readings.
claims.limits: Educational explanation only. No historical copying connections among the desk’s selected witnesses are asserted.

researchDevelopments.earlier: Monier (2019) supported treating GA 304 as a witness to ending at 16:8; Head (June 2022) cites that research.
researchDevelopments.later: Houghton (online December 2022; issue January 2023) argues that the manuscript is unfinished.
researchDevelopments.significance: Read a witness’s production and commentary context before using its last biblical words as evidence. The revision changes one supporting datum, not the broader consensus.

researchDevelopments.earlier: Compact editions compare selected textual alternatives.
researchDevelopments.later: ECM documents extensive Greek, versional and patristic evidence; CBGM adds explicit hypotheses about variant relationships.
researchDevelopments.significance: Increased documentation can reveal uncertainty as well as support decisions.

traditionsAndLimits.greek: Papyri, majuscule codices, corrections and Byzantine catena production all contribute different kinds of evidence.
traditionsAndLimits.versions: Latin, Syriac and Coptic are introduced through ECM scope and ancient transmission. No new versional readings displayed: translating back into Greek is not mechanically reliable.
traditionsAndLimits.geography: The objects’ modern custodians are not assumed to be their ancient places of copying. Scholarship consulted spans Michigan, Münster, Birmingham, Cambridge and Uppsala; ancient testimony includes Irenaeus and Eusebius.
traditionsAndLimits.hebrewBible: Not covered by these examples; no assertion that all biblical textual traditions follow the same editorial history.
traditionsAndLimits.theology: Canonical authority and inspiration require interpretive commitments beyond identifying the earliest attainable wording. The study explains textual claims without resolving denominational reception.

openResearchGaps: Romans corrected hands remain apparatus-based reports; exact physical forms and correction chronology await direct visual collation.
GA 304 classification follows Houghton. The original object and its erased epigram were not freshly inspected; Monier’s 2019 paper was blocked at the repository.
Full ECM explanatory volumes and Parker’s full book remain unread. Historical edition readings are verified through the SBLGNT comparative apparatus.
The full range of translated Mark endings, combined endings and Freer Logion is not collated here.
No surviving evidence can identify with certainty the lost exemplar or interrupted copying event behind GA 304.
